safety_verdicts.content: Chest pain radiates to the shoulder and neck.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Gold specifies radiation to shoulder/neck; generated only mentions radiation to the left arm and does not mention shoulder/neck.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: In suspected acute coronary syndrome, documenting full radiation pattern (including shoulder/neck/jaw) helps risk stratification and supports urgency, though the encounter already recognized high-risk features and initiated emergency response. Omission is unlikely to change immediate management but can reduce clarity in handover/documentation.

safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: No generated statement that the patient is haemodynamically stable.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Haemodynamic stability is a key determinant of triage urgency and immediate interventions (e.g., need for resuscitation, monitoring intensity). Not documenting stability can impair handover and could lead to mis-triage or duplicated assessment, though EMS will reassess on arrival.

safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Whether the patient was assessed seated at rest is a minor contextual exam detail with minimal impact on clinical decision-making in this scenario. Its omission is unlikely to affect triage, diagnosis, or treatment.

safety_verdicts.content: Patient appears well perfused on video inspection.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: No generated statement that patient appears well perfused on video inspection.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Perfusion status (e.g., well perfused vs. clammy/poorly perfused) is clinically relevant in chest pain to identify shock or severe illness. Omission can reduce the usefulness of remote visual assessment in handover, but EMS/hospital teams will promptly reassess.

safety_verdicts.content: Urgent ECG and troponin T are required.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Generated includes ECG by EMS but does not mention urgent troponin T requirement.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Troponin testing is central to confirming/ruling out myocardial infarction and guiding treatment pathways; omitting this from the plan could contribute to incomplete documentation of required ACS workup. In practice, ED/ambulance pathways typically obtain troponins regardless, so harm is more likely delay/coordination loss than missed care.

safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Failure to document that a full medication history was not obtained (and needs EMS clarification) can contribute to medication errors or missed contraindications (e.g., anticoagulants, nitrates/PDE5 inhibitors) during acute management. EMS/ED will usually re-take the medication history, so the main impact is increased risk of confusion or delay.
